items.q: For a saturated clay loaded so fast that no water can escape (φ<sub>u</sub> = 0), the Hansen bearing capacity factors are
items.why: φ = 0 gives N<sub>q</sub> = e<sup>π tanφ</sup>tan²(45° + φ/2) = 1, N<sub>γ</sub> = 1.8(N<sub>q</sub> − 1)tanφ = 0 and N<sub>c</sub> = π + 2 = 5.14.

items.q: In q<sub>f</sub> = cN<sub>c</sub> + γDN<sub>q</sub> + ½γBN<sub>γ</sub> the middle term represents

options.A: the cohesion of the soil under the footing
options.B: the surcharge from the soil beside the footing
options.C: the weight of the footing itself
options.D: the self-weight of the soil under the footing

items.why: The three terms are cohesion (cN<sub>c</sub>), surcharge from the soil at the base level (γDN<sub>q</sub>) and the weight of soil in the failure wedge (½γBN<sub>γ</sub>).

items.q: For a footing in sand with c = 0, doubling the footing width B (same depth, same soil) changes the capacity as follows

options.B: q<sub>f</sub> is unchanged because it is a pressure
options.C: Only the ½γBN<sub>γ</sub> term doubles; the γDN<sub>q</sub> term is unchanged

items.why: B appears only in the unit-weight term. The surcharge term depends on the depth D, so total q<sub>f</sub> rises by less than a factor of 2.

items.q: The net ultimate bearing capacity is defined as
items.why: The soil that was excavated already carried γD, so only the pressure above it counts: q<sub>nf</sub> = q<sub>f</sub> − γD.

items.q: The factor of safety against shear failure used in the tutorials is

options.A: F = q<sub>nf</sub> / q<sub>n</sub>, net capacity over net applied pressure
options.D: F = q<sub>f</sub> / q<sub>applied</sub>, gross over gross, always

items.why: Both capacity and applied pressure are taken net of γD: F = q<sub>nf</sub>/q<sub>n</sub>. (Gross over gross is also seen, but it is not the tutorial convention.)

items.q: A strip footing 2 m wide at 1.5 m depth in saturated clay (c<sub>u</sub> = 40 kPa, φ<sub>u</sub> = 0, γ = 18 kN/m³) carries 150 kN/m. The factor of safety (Hansen, N<sub>c</sub> = 5.14) is about
items.why: q<sub>nf</sub> = c<sub>u</sub>N<sub>c</sub> = 205.6 kPa; q<sub>n</sub> = Q/B − γD = 75 − 27 = 48 kPa; F = 205.6/48 = 4.3.

items.q: A 2 m square footing at 1 m depth in dry sand (c = 0, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°). Take N<sub>q</sub> = 18.4 and N<sub>γ</sub> = 18.1. Using the simplified shape factors, q<sub>f</sub> is about
items.why: Square: q<sub>f</sub> = γDN<sub>q</sub> + 0.4γBN<sub>γ</sub> = 331 + 261 = 592 kPa. (½ is for a strip; 574 is the net value.)

items.q: The simplified shape factors for a square footing in the unit-weight and cohesion terms are
items.why: Square: s<sub>γ</sub> = 0.8 (so 0.4γBN<sub>γ</sub>), s<sub>c</sub> = 1.3, s<sub>q</sub> = 1. Circular: 0.3γBN<sub>γ</sub> with s<sub>c</sub> = 1.3.

items.q: In a saturated sand with the water table at the ground surface, which unit weight goes into q<sub>f</sub> = γDN<sub>q</sub> + ½γBN<sub>γ</sub>?

options.A: γ′ = γ<sub>sat</sub> − γ<sub>w</sub> in both terms
options.C: γ′ in the first term and γ<sub>sat</sub> in the second

items.why: Both the soil beside the footing and the soil under it are submerged, so both terms carry the buoyant unit weight.

items.q: Dry sand above a water table that rests exactly at the footing base. In q<sub>f</sub> = γDN<sub>q</sub> + ½γBN<sub>γ</sub>

options.A: the first term uses γ′ and the second keeps γ
options.B: the first term keeps γ and the second uses γ′

items.why: The surcharge term involves the soil above the base, which is above the water table, so γ. The wedge below the base is submerged, so γ′.

items.q: The water table need not be considered for bearing capacity (the soil is treated as dry) when it is deeper than about

options.A: the footing length L below the ground
options.B: the footing depth D below the ground
options.C: 1.5 to 2 times the footing width below the base
options.D: 0.5 times the footing width below the base

items.why: The failure wedge extends about 1.5 to 2B below the base. Below that depth the water table does not touch it.

items.q: A strip footing in saturated sand (γ<sub>sat</sub> = 20 kN/m³, γ<sub>w</sub> = 9.81 kN/m³, c = 0) has the water table at the surface. The weight to use in both q<sub>f</sub> terms is
A strip footing 3 m wide carries a vertical load at an eccentricity e = 0.4 m. The effective width is
items.why: B′ = B − 2e = 3 − 0.8 = 2.2 m. The load acts on the middle part that is symmetric about it.

items.q: For an inclined load with V = 300 kN/m and H = 60 kN/m, i<sub>q</sub> = 1 − 1.5H/V. The factor on the unit-weight term, i<sub>γ</sub> = i<sub>q</sub>², is
items.why: i<sub>q</sub> = 1 − 1.5·60/300 = 0.7; i<sub>γ</sub> = i<sub>q</sub>² = 0.49. The unit-weight term is cut more than the surcharge term.

items.q: Which soil parameters should a stability check immediately after construction of a footing on saturated clay use?
items.why: Clay loaded quickly cannot drain, so the short-term case is undrained with total-stress parameters. The long-term check uses c′ and φ′.

items.q: Which of these is not an assumption of Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory?

options.A: The failure is by general shear
options.B: The base of the footing is rough
options.C: The overburden is replaced by a surcharge γD
options.D: The soil is layered, anisotropic and the load is inclined

items.why: Terzaghi assumes a homogeneous, isotropic, semi-infinite soil, a vertical symmetric load on a strip, a rough base, general shear and a surcharge γD. Layers and inclination need extensions.

items.q: A foundation is classed as shallow when, in the lecture, its depth-to-width ratio

options.C: D is below the water table

items.why: The course treats a footing or raft as shallow when D/B < 1; piles are deep (L/D large).

items.q: Load-settlement behaviour with a well-defined peak, heave of the ground on both sides and tilting of the footing indicates
items.why: General shear: a continuous failure surface reaches the ground surface; typical of dense sand or stiff clay.

items.q: Large settlements, no heave away from the footing and no tilting, with a load-settlement curve that has no clear peak, are typical of

options.D: a stiff clay under a surface strip

items.why: Punching: the soil is compressible (loose) or the footing is deep; the footing sinks as a plug with vertical shearing at its edges.

items.q: Which pair is correct?

options.A: Local shear: a clear peak load and large heave on both sides
options.B: Punching: continuous slip surface to the ground and tilting
options.C: General shear: footing punches vertically with no heave
options.D: Local shear: failure surfaces do not reach the surface, only slight heave, ultimate load not well defined

items.why: Local shear sits between general and punching: significant compression, slip surfaces that do not reach the surface, slight heave.

items.q: Excavations in soft clay can fail by bottom heave. For φ = 0 the factor of safety against heave is

options.A: F = c<sub>u</sub>N<sub>c</sub> / (γD), plus the surcharge q<sub>s</sub> in the denominator if there is one

items.why: The bearing pressure is c<sub>u</sub>N<sub>c</sub>; the pressure driving failure is the weight of clay beside the excavation, γD (+ q<sub>s</sub> for a surcharge).

items.q: A 6 m deep excavation in clay (c<sub>u</sub> = 30 kPa, γ = 17 kN/m³, φ = 0) has no surcharge. The factor of safety against bottom heave (N<sub>c</sub> = 5.14) is
Which pair names the two limit states every foundation design must satisfy?

options.C: Ultimate limit state (collapse) and serviceability limit state (excessive deformation)

items.why: ULS: the soil must not fail in shear. SLS: settlement must not harm the structure or its function.

items.q: Raft foundations are chosen over separate footings mainly when

options.A: the soil is very dense rock
options.D: the soil bearing capacity is low or the columns are so close that footings would overlap

items.why: A raft spreads load, lowers contact pressure and reduces differential settlement on weak or variable soil.

items.q: The bearing capacity factors N<sub>q</sub>, N<sub>c</sub> and N<sub>γ</sub> increase rapidly with φ. When φ increases from 30° to 40° (Hansen), N<sub>q</sub> roughly
items.why: N<sub>q</sub> = 18.4 at 30° and 64.2 at 40°; N<sub>γ</sub> rises even faster (18 to 95). Small errors in φ change q<sub>f</sub> a lot.

items.q: In the standard penetration test the blow count N is the number of blows for the

options.B: last two 150 mm increments (300 mm) of a 450 mm drive

items.why: The first 150 mm is seating; N is the sum of the second and third 150 mm. The hammer is 63.5 kg dropped 760 mm.

items.q: A SPT with an energy ratio of 75 % gives N = 20. Corrected to the standard 60 % energy, N<sub>60</sub> is
The overburden correction factor C<sub>N</sub> is larger for a test at

options.A: a depth just below the water table only
options.B: the same value at all depths

items.why: High confining stress inflates N, so deep tests are scaled down; C<sub>N</sub> falls as σ′ rises and exceeds 1 near the surface.

items.q: The dilatancy correction N′ = 15 + ½(N<sub>1</sub> − 15) is applied

options.A: to fine or silty sand below the water table when N<sub>1</sub> > 15
options.B: to clean gravel above the water table

items.why: In saturated fine sand the pore pressure cannot dissipate in the blow, so counts above 15 read too high and are reduced.

items.q: Fine saturated sand below the water table gives N<sub>1</sub> = 25 after the overburden correction. The dilatancy-corrected count is
The order of the corrections in tutorial 2 Q2 is

options.C: energy to N<sub>60</sub>, then overburden (C<sub>N</sub>), then dilatancy if N<sub>1</sub> > 15

items.why: Each step uses the result of the one before; dilatancy needs the overburden-corrected N<sub>1</sub>.

items.q: A square footing B = 2 m at D = 1 m; the water table is 1.5 m below the surface. The water table correction C<sub>w</sub> = 0.5 + 0.5D<sub>w</sub>/(D + B) is
The water table correction on allowable bearing pressure is 0.5 when the water table is

options.A: at the ground surface (or at the base for a surface footing)
options.B: at a depth B below the base

items.why: C<sub>w</sub> falls linearly from 1 (water table ≥ B below the base) to 0.5 (at the ground level). In the 2026 paper Q4 the base is the surface.

items.q: A plate load test (0.3 m plate) on sand settles 8 mm at a given pressure. A 1.5 m square footing at that pressure settles about
items.why: Sand: s = s<sub>p</sub>[2B/(B + B<sub>p</sub>)]² = 8·2.78 = 22.2 mm. A direct ratio of widths (40 mm) is the clay rule, not the sand rule.

items.q: A plate load test (0.305 m plate) on clay settles 6 mm under a given pressure. The settlement of a 1.525 m wide footing at that pressure is about
items.why: In clay the settlement scales with width: s = s<sub>p</sub>·B/B<sub>p</sub> = 6 × 1.525/0.305 = 30 mm.

items.q: A plate load test can give a misleading result because

options.B: the water table has no effect on it
options.D: the plate stresses only a shallow zone (about 2B<sub>p</sub>) and misses weak layers deeper down

items.why: A 0.3 m plate loads a zone about 0.6 m deep; the real footing stresses a much deeper zone, so a weak layer below goes unseen.

items.q: The allowable bearing pressure of a foundation depends on

options.A: both the ultimate bearing capacity and the allowable settlement: the smaller of the two controls
options.C: neither; it is fixed by the code

items.why: q<sub>a</sub> is the lesser of q<sub>nf</sub>/F and the pressure that keeps settlement within the limit. On sand the settlement limit usually governs.

items.q: The standard CPT uses a cone with

options.B: 60° apex, 1000 mm² end area, pushed at 20 mm/s
options.C: 30° apex, 1000 mm² end area, pushed at 2 mm/s

items.why: Standard cone: diameter 35.7 mm, 10 cm² end area, 60° tip, 20 mm/s; it measures q<sub>c</sub>, f<sub>s</sub> and u.

items.q: Using q<sub>c</sub> (MN/m²) = 0.4N (Meyerhof 1956), a layer with N = 15 has a cone resistance of about
items.why: q<sub>c</sub> = 0.4 × 15 = 6 MN/m².

items.q: A limitation of the CPT, compared with the SPT, is that

options.A: it gives only isolated values with depth
options.C: it depends strongly on the operator
options.D: it cannot penetrate gravels or cobbles and gives no sample

items.why: CPT gives continuous, repeatable profiles without boring but cannot push through coarse gravel or cobbles, and takes no sample.

items.q: On sand, s = s<sub>p</sub>[2B/(B + B<sub>p</sub>)]². For a footing much wider than the plate (B ≫ B<sub>p</sub>) the ratio s/s<sub>p</sub> tends to
items.why: As B ≫ B<sub>p</sub>, 2B/(B + B<sub>p</sub>) → 2, so the ratio → 4: settlement grows with width on sand, but saturates at about 4 times the plate value.

items.q: Coarse-grained soils settle mainly by
items.why: Their permeability is high, so pore water drains at once; the settlement is essentially immediate.

items.q: A flexible footing: q = 100 kPa, B = 2 m, ν = 0.5, I<sub>f</sub> = 0.56, E = 20 MPa. s<sub>i</sub> = qB(1 − ν²)I<sub>f</sub>/E is about
In Burland's s<sub>i</sub> = μ<sub>0</sub>μ<sub>1</sub>qB/E<sub>u</sub>

options.A: μ₀ allows for the layer thickness and μ₁ for the embedment depth
options.D: μ₀ allows for the depth of embedment and μ₁ for the layer thickness and shape of the loaded area

items.why: μ<sub>0</sub> depends on D/B (embedment); μ<sub>1</sub> on H/B and L/B.

items.q: For a layered clay, the immediate settlement is found by superposition. The usual pattern is

options.A: s = s₁(upper, E₁) + s₂(both layers, E₂) − s₃(upper, E₂)
options.D: the average of s₁ and s₂

items.why: Count the soft upper layer with its own E, add the whole stack with E₂, and remove the upper part counted twice (with E₂).

items.q: The mean settlement of a rigid foundation is commonly taken as about

options.B: 0.8 times the centre settlement of the same flexible foundation

items.why: The rigidity factor 0.8 reduces the flexible centre settlement to the mean value of a rigid footing.

items.q: The three components of foundation settlement, in the order they develop, are
items.why: Elastic: on loading. Primary: as excess pore pressure dissipates. Secondary: creep after the pore pressure has gone.

items.q: The pre-consolidation pressure σ′<sub>pc</sub> is

options.A: the pore pressure at the clay mid-depth
options.C: the stress at which the clay fails
options.D: the greatest vertical effective stress the soil has ever carried

items.why: Below it the clay re-compresses stiffly (C<sub>r</sub>); beyond it, virgin compression (C<sub>c</sub>).

items.q: A clay with OCR < 1 is

options.A: under-consolidated, still consolidating under its present load

items.why: OCR = σ′<sub>c</sub>/σ′<sub>0</sub>. OCR = 1 normally consolidated, > 1 over-consolidated, < 1 under-consolidated (σ′<sub>0</sub> > σ′<sub>c</sub>).

items.q: The recompression index C<sub>r</sub> is compared with the compression index C<sub>c</sub> as

options.B: much smaller (the re-compression line is flat)

items.why: The e–log σ′ curve is flat below p<sub>c</sub> (C<sub>r</sub>, often a fifth to a tenth of C<sub>c</sub>) and steeper beyond it.

items.q: A clay with C<sub>c</sub> = 0.4 and C<sub>r</sub> = 0.05 has e = 1.2, σ′<sub>0</sub> = 50 kPa, p<sub>c</sub> = 100 kPa and is loaded to 190 kPa. The final void ratio is about
items.why: Re-compress to p<sub>c</sub> with C<sub>r</sub>: 0.0151; then virgin to 190: 0.1115. Δe = 0.127, e<sub>f</sub> = 1.073.

items.q: The initial and final void ratios in a consolidation test are 1.0 and 0.5. The sample was 2.4 cm thick at the start. Its final thickness is
items.why: The solids height is constant: H ∝ (1 + e). H<sub>f</sub> = 2.4·1.5/2.0 = 1.8 cm.

items.q: A saturated clay has w = 40 % and G<sub>s</sub> = 2.7. Its void ratio is
Terzaghi and Peck estimate C<sub>c</sub> = 0.009(w<sub>L</sub> − 10) for undisturbed clay. For w<sub>L</sub> = 60 %, C<sub>c</sub> is
items.why: C<sub>c</sub> = 0.009·50 = 0.45 (0.007 is the remoulded relation).

items.q: A normally consolidated clay layer 4 m thick: C<sub>c</sub> = 0.3, e<sub>0</sub> = 1.0. The effective stress at mid-depth rises from 100 to 200 kPa. The consolidation settlement is about
items.why: S<sub>c</sub> = C<sub>c</sub>H/(1 + e<sub>0</sub>)·log(σ′<sub>f</sub>/σ′<sub>0</sub>) = 0.3·4/2·0.301 = 0.181 m = 181 mm.

items.q: An over-consolidated clay, H = 2 m, e<sub>0</sub> = 0.9, C<sub>r</sub> = 0.05, C<sub>c</sub> = 0.4, σ′<sub>0</sub> = 50 kPa, p<sub>c</sub> = 100 kPa, σ′<sub>f</sub> = 200 kPa. The settlement is about
items.why: Two parts: C<sub>r</sub>log(p<sub>c</sub>/σ′<sub>0</sub>) = 0.0151 and C<sub>c</sub>log(σ′<sub>f</sub>/p<sub>c</sub>) = 0.1204; S<sub>c</sub> = H/(1 + e<sub>0</sub>)·sum = 143 mm.

items.q: A normally consolidated, saturated silty clay 1 m thick, specific gravity 2.7, w = 45 %, C<sub>c</sub> = 0.45, σ′<sub>0</sub> = 100 kPa, Δσ = 20 kPa. The primary settlement is
items.why: e<sub>0</sub> = wG<sub>s</sub> = 1.215; S = 0.45·1/(2.215)·log(120/100) = 16 mm. (Using C<sub>r</sub> instead of C<sub>c</sub> would give about 2 mm.)

items.q: The coefficient of volume compressibility of a clay is m<sub>v</sub> = 0.4 m²/MN. A 5 m layer takes an effective stress increase of 80 kPa. The settlement is
items.why: S = m<sub>v</sub>Δσ′H. Convert m<sub>v</sub> to m²/kN: 0.4/1000 = 0.0004. S = 0.0004·80·5 = 0.16 m = 160 mm. The unit change is the trap.

items.q: The water table in a thick sand over a 5 m clay layer is lowered 4 m by pumping; total stress at the clay does not change. γ<sub>w</sub> = 9.81 kN/m³. The effective stress in the clay rises by about

options.D: 0 kPa (the water table does not matter)

items.why: The pore pressure falls by γ<sub>w</sub>Δh = 39.2 kPa; with total stress unchanged, σ′ rises by the same.

items.q: Clay settles when it is dewatered (for example by groundwater pumping) because

options.D: the effective stress on the clay increases

items.why: Lower pore pressure means higher effective stress, which compresses the clay.

items.q: On an e–log σ′<sub>v</sub> plot the slope of the straight virgin line is

options.C: the coefficient of volume compressibility m<sub>v</sub>

items.why: C<sub>c</sub> = −Δe/Δlog σ′. The others are not slopes of that plot.

items.q: Estimating σ′<sub>pc</sub> from an oedometer curve is most affected by

options.B: sample disturbance, which rounds the curve and lowers the apparent p<sub>c</sub>

items.why: Disturbed samples give a rounded e–log σ′ curve, and p<sub>c</sub> is hard to read; a systematic error towards a low value.

items.q: The vertical stress under a point load Q at depth z and radial distance r is σ<sub>z</sub> = I<sub>p</sub>Q/z². I<sub>p</sub> is largest

options.C: directly under the load (r = 0), where I<sub>p</sub> = 3/(2π) ≈ 0.48
options.D: at the depth z = 0 and any r

items.why: Boussinesq: I<sub>p</sub> = 3/(2π)·[1/(1 + (r/z)²)]<sup>5/2</sup>, maximum 0.477 at r = 0.

items.q: A point load of 500 kN acts on the surface of an elastic half-space. The vertical stress directly below it at 2 m depth (I<sub>p</sub> = 0.478) is about
The influence-factor chart for a rectangular area (m = B/z, n = L/z) gives the stress

options.A: under a corner of the loaded rectangle
options.B: under the centre of the rectangle

items.why: Fadum's I<sub>σ</sub> is for the corner. For other points divide the area into rectangles that share the point as a corner.

items.q: A 4 × 4 m square carries q = 100 kPa. Using Iσ = 0.175 for m = n = 1, the vertical stress at 2 m depth under its centre is about
items.why: Split into four 2 × 2 squares with a corner at the centre; m = n = 2/2 = 1, I<sub>σ</sub> = 0.175 each. σ<sub>z</sub> = 4·0.175·100 = 70 kPa.

items.q: To find the stress at a point A outside the loaded rectangle, with A on the centre line 1.5 m outside a long edge, the working uses

options.A: one rectangle with the largest m
options.B: the stress at the centre times 0.5
options.C: two large rectangles (A to the far edge) minus two small rectangles (A to the near edge)
options.D: the point-load formula for the whole area

items.why: Rectangles sharing corner A: large ones (loaded + gap) minus the small ones (gap only), doubled by symmetry. σ<sub>z</sub> = 2q(I<sub>1</sub> − I<sub>2</sub>).

items.q: In the Skempton–Bjerrum method, s<sub>c</sub> = μ s<sub>oed</sub> with μ = A + α(1 − A). The factor μ corrects for

options.D: lateral strain in the field, which the oedometer test prevents

items.why: The oedometer has zero lateral strain; in the field the initial pore pressure depends on A, and μ (about 0.5 to 1) adjusts s<sub>oed</sub>.

items.q: Which is not an assumption of Terzaghi's one-dimensional consolidation theory?

options.B: The soil is homogeneous and saturated
options.C: Darcy's law is valid and flow is one-dimensional
options.D: Water and solid particles are incompressible

items.why: The theory needs a saturated soil; the others are standard assumptions.

items.q: Increasing the permeability of a clay, others unchanged,

options.B: raises c<sub>v</sub> = k/(γ<sub>w</sub>m<sub>v</sub>) and shortens the time to consolidate

items.why: c<sub>v</sub> = k/(γ<sub>w</sub>m<sub>v</sub>); t = T<sub>v</sub>H²/c<sub>v</sub>. Higher k, higher c<sub>v</sub>, shorter t. The stress increase does not enter c<sub>v</sub> or T<sub>v</sub>.

items.q: The time factor is

options.C: T<sub>v</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>t/H<sub>dr</sub>², with H<sub>dr</sub> the longest drainage path

items.why: H<sub>dr</sub> is H for single drainage, H/2 for drainage at top and bottom.

items.q: For U < 60 % the time factor is T<sub>v</sub> = (π/4)U². At U = 50 %, T<sub>v</sub> is about
For U > 60 %, T<sub>v</sub> = 1.781 − 0.933 log(100 − U%). At U = 90 %, T<sub>v</sub> is
A 2 cm clay sample with double drainage reaches 50 % consolidation in 5 min. A field layer of the same clay, 2 m thick with double drainage, will take
items.why: t ∝ H<sub>dr</sub>²; the thickness ratio is 200/2 = 100; t = 5·100² = 50 000 min ≈ 34.7 days.

items.q: The same clay layer is first drained at the top and bottom, then at the top only. The time to reach the same U becomes
items.why: H<sub>dr</sub> doubles when one drain is removed; t ∝ H<sub>dr</sub>².

items.q: A 2 cm sample with double drainage reaches 50 % in 10 min (T<sub>50</sub> = 0.197). The coefficient of consolidation is
items.why: H<sub>dr</sub> = 1 cm; c<sub>v</sub> = 0.197·1²/600 s = 3.28 × 10⁻⁴ cm²/s. (Using 2 cm as the path gives four times more.)

items.q: A clay is 11.43 cm settled at 4 years from mid-loading (ultimate 35.565 cm). At 9 years from the same datum, assuming U < 60 %, it will have settled
In Taylor's square-root-of-time method the 90 % point is found by drawing a line whose abscissa is

options.B: 1.15 times that of the initial straight line
options.C: 2 times that of the initial straight line
options.D: 0.5 times that of the initial straight line

items.why: Line d<sub>0</sub>B with d<sub>0</sub>B = 1.15·d<sub>0</sub>A meets the curve at √t<sub>90</sub>, and T<sub>90</sub> = 0.848.

items.q: Vertical drains (PVDs) speed consolidation because they

options.A: reduce the compressibility of the soil
options.C: shorten the drainage path and make the flow horizontal

items.why: The drainage distance becomes half the drain spacing, orders of magnitude shorter than the layer thickness, and t ∝ d².

items.q: More compressible clay (higher m<sub>v</sub>), other properties equal, has

options.D: a lower c<sub>v</sub> and consolidates more slowly

items.why: c<sub>v</sub> = k/(γ<sub>w</sub>m<sub>v</sub>): a more compressible clay has more water to expel for the same permeability, so t = T<sub>v</sub>H²/c<sub>v</sub> grows.

items.q: Secondary compression is

options.A: settlement that continues after the excess pore pressure has dissipated, linear in log time
options.B: settlement caused by the water table dropping
options.C: settlement under the first load increment only

items.why: S<sub>s</sub> = C<sub>α</sub>H log(t/t<sub>p</sub>)/(1 + e<sub>p</sub>) after primary is complete.

items.q: A clay layer 8 m thick has C<sub>αε</sub> = 1 % (strain per log cycle) and primary consolidation ends at t<sub>p</sub> = 1 yr. The secondary compression by t = 10 yr is
items.why: S<sub>s</sub> = C<sub>αε</sub>H log(t/t<sub>p</sub>) = 0.01·8·log 10 = 0.08 m = 80 mm. One log cycle gives C<sub>αε</sub>H.

items.q: The secondary compression index C<sub>αε</sub> relates to C<sub>α</sub> by
items.why: C<sub>α</sub> is Δe per log cycle; dividing by 1 + e<sub>p</sub> turns it into strain per log cycle.

items.q: For a normally consolidated clay, the ratio C<sub>α</sub>/C<sub>c</sub> is roughly constant: about

options.D: 0.04 for inorganic clays and a little more for organic soils

items.why: Mesri and co-workers found C<sub>α</sub>/C<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.04 ± 0.01 for inorganic clays and silts and ≈ 0.05 for organic ones (external; not in the lecture).

items.q: Meyerhof (1965), B > 1.25 m: s<sub>L</sub> = (q<sub>a</sub>·2.24/N)[B/(B + 0.33)]². For N = 15, B = 2 m, s<sub>L</sub> = 25 mm, q<sub>a</sub> is about
In Schmertmann's method, for a square footing the modulus of each layer is estimated as
items.why: The lecture gives E = 2.5q<sub>c</sub> for L/B = 1 and 3.5q<sub>c</sub> for L/B ≥ 10.

items.q: For a square footing the strain influence factor Iz is

options.B: peak at the base, zero at B/2
options.C: 0.1 at the base, peak I<sub>zp</sub> at B/2 below it, zero at 2B
options.D: 0 at the base, peak at 2B, 0.1 at depth

items.why: Schmertmann's triangle: 0.1 at z = 0, peak at z = B/2, zero at z = 2B (strip: peak at B, zero at 4B).

items.q: The peak strain influence factor I<sub>zp</sub> = 0.5 + 0.1√(q<sub>n</sub>/σ′<sub>vp</sub>). For q<sub>n</sub> = 150 kPa and σ′<sub>vp</sub> = 37.5 kPa it is
items.why: √(150/37.5) = 2; I<sub>zp</sub> = 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.70. σ′<sub>vp</sub> is at the depth of the peak (B/2 below the base).

items.q: The depth correction is C<sub>1</sub> = 1 − 0.5σ′<sub>v0</sub>/q<sub>n</sub>. For σ′<sub>v0</sub> = 20 kPa and q<sub>n</sub> = 100 kPa, C<sub>1</sub> is
items.why: 1 − 0.5·20/100 = 0.90. Deeper footings are stiffer: less settlement.

items.q: The creep factor C<sub>2</sub> = 1 + 0.2 log(t/0.1), t in years. For t = 10 years it is
items.why: 1 + 0.2·log(100) = 1.4. With no time given, C<sub>2</sub> = 1.

items.q: One layer 2 m thick with q<sub>c</sub> = 4 MPa, mid-layer I<sub>z</sub> = 0.5, q<sub>n</sub> = 100 kPa, C<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub> = 1 (square footing, E = 2.5q<sub>c</sub>). The settlement is
items.why: s = qn·I<sub>z</sub>Δz/E = 100 kPa·0.5·2 m/10 MPa = 10 mm (kPa·m/MPa gives mm).

items.q: The net ultimate bearing capacity of a purely cohesive soil

options.A: Depends on the width of the footing and is independent of the depth of the footing
options.B: Depends on the width as well as the depth of the footing
options.C: Depends on the depth, but is independent of the width of the footing
options.D: Is independent of both the width and the depth of the footing

items.why: φ<sub>u</sub> = 0 gives N<sub>q</sub> = 1 and N<sub>γ</sub> = 0, so q<sub>net</sub> = c<sub>u</sub>N<sub>c</sub>: no B and no D are left.

items.q: Two footings, one circular and the other square, are founded on the surface of a purely cohesionless soil. The diameter of the circular footing is the same as the side of the square footing. Then q<sub>f</sub>(circular)/q<sub>f</sub>(square) is:
items.why: Cohesionless surface footing: only the N<sub>γ</sub> term is left. 0.3γBN<sub>γ</sub> (circle) over 0.4γBN<sub>γ</sub> (square) = 3/4.

items.q: A granular soil was subjected to standard penetration tests at a depth of 3 m. Ground water level was 1.5 m below the surface; the soil was saturated with unit weight 19.3 kN/m³ (18 kN/m³ above the water table). The average N value was 15. What is the corrected value of N for overburden pressure?
items.flag: Formula-dependent: √(100/σ′) gives 23.4, so C (25); Peck 0.77·log(1915/σ′) gives 19.3, so B (20). Check which C<sub>N</sub> the course uses.

items.q: The allowable bearing pressure for a square footing 1.5 m × 1.5 m resting on the surface of a sand deposit was estimated as 600 kN/m² (field test) with the water table well below the base. What are the allowable bearing capacities (kN/m²) when the water level rises to 3 m, 1.5 m and 0.0 m below the base?
items.why: A water table deeper than B below the base has no effect (600); at the base it halves the capacity (300); 1.5 m = B below the base has no effect (600).

items.q: A layer of normally consolidated, saturated silty clay 1 m thick is subjected to one-dimensional consolidation under a pressure increment of 20 kPa. G<sub>s</sub> = 2.7, natural moisture content 45 %, C<sub>c</sub> = 0.45, C<sub>r</sub> = 0.05, initial average effective stress 100 kPa. Assuming Terzaghi's theory, the primary consolidation settlement (nearest mm) is:
items.why: e<sub>0</sub> = wG<sub>s</sub> = 1.215; s = C<sub>c</sub>/(1 + e<sub>0</sub>)·H·log(120/100) = 16 mm.

items.q:
Consider the following statements:
[1] Consolidation time increases with increasing compressibility
[2] Consolidation time decreases with increasing permeability
[3] Consolidation time is dependent on the magnitude of stress increase
Which of these statements are correct?
items.why: More compressible (m<sub>v</sub> up) lowers c<sub>v</sub> so it is slower; more permeable is faster; the stress increase does not enter c<sub>v</sub>.
items.flag: Strict Terzaghi theory: time does not depend on the stress increase (B); some keys give A.

items.q: During the consolidation of a clay layer, if instead of double drainage the drainage is allowed at a single face only, the rate of compression will be
items.why: t ∝ d². Single drainage doubles the drainage path, so it is 4 times slower.

items.q: The slope of the e–log σ′<sub>v</sub> curve for a soil mass gives
items.why: The slope of void ratio against log effective stress is C<sub>c</sub>.

Match: P: Curve J, Q: Curve K, R: Curve L with 1: No apparent heaving of soil around the footing; 2: Rankine's passive zone develops imperfectly; 3: Well defined slip surface extends to the ground surface.
items.why: J (sharp peak) is general shear with a slip surface to the ground; K is local shear; L (no peak) is punching with no heave. The figure is not reproduced here: see the paper.

items.q: For the determination of the shear strength parameters c and φ of soil in the laboratory, the test to be conducted will be
items.why: c and φ come from a triaxial (or direct shear) test.

items.q: The bearing capacity factors N<sub>c</sub>, N<sub>q</sub> and N<sub>γ</sub> are functions of

options.D: Angle of internal friction of soil

items.why: N<sub>c</sub>, N<sub>q</sub> and N<sub>γ</sub> depend only on φ.

items.q: A footing rests on the surface or at shallow depth in a very dense sand. Which type of failure is likely?
items.why: Very dense sand with a shallow footing gives general shear.

items.q: The allowable bearing pressure for a foundation depends upon

options.B: Ultimate bearing capacity of the soil only
options.C: Both allowable settlement and ultimate bearing capacity

items.why: It is the lesser of q<sub>ult</sub>/F and the pressure that gives the allowable settlement.
